stem: You ran `git add config.yml` by mistake. You want the file **unstaged** but your edits to it kept in the working tree. Which command does exactly that in Git 2.4x?

options.text: `git restore --staged config.yml`
options.why: It copies the HEAD version into the index only, so the change becomes unstaged but stays on disk.

options.text: `git restore config.yml`
options.why: Without `--staged` it restores the working tree from the index, which would overwrite your edits.

options.text: `git reset --hard config.yml`
options.why: Hard reset does not accept paths, and on the whole tree it would discard your edits.

options.text: `git rm config.yml` to take it out of the next commit
options.why: This stages a deletion and removes the file from disk; it does not unstage anything.

explanation: `git restore --staged <path>` resets the index entry to match HEAD and leaves the working tree untouched, which is the modern spelling of `git reset <path>`. `git status` even suggests it under "Changes to be committed".

stem: `git reset --hard` deletes untracked files (files Git has never been told about) from the working tree.

options.text: True
options.why: Untracked files are not in the index or HEAD, so reset has nothing to reset them to and leaves them alone.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: reset --hard only rewrites tracked paths. Untracked (and ignored) files survive; `git clean` removes them.

explanation: Running `reset --hard` against a dirty tree in Git 2.55 restored the tracked file and left `untracked.txt` and an ignored `x.log` in place. One subtle exception: a file that was **staged but never committed** is tracked in the index, so `reset --hard` does delete it.

stem: You have edits to tracked files **and** a brand-new untracked file. Type the complete `git stash` command (one flag) that saves both so the working tree is clean.
explanation: By default `git stash` saves only tracked changes (staged and unstaged); untracked files stay behind. `-u` / `--include-untracked` adds them to the stash, and `-a` / `--all` also includes ignored files.

stem: A commit you pushed to the shared `main` branch an hour ago introduced a bug. Teammates have already pulled it. What is the safest way to undo its changes?

options.text: `git reset --hard HEAD~1` followed by a normal `git push`
options.why: The push is rejected as non-fast-forward, and forcing it would rewrite history others already have.

options.text: `git revert <sha>` and push the new commit
options.why: Revert adds a new commit that applies the inverse change, so shared history is only added to.

options.text: `git commit --amend` and push again
options.why: Amend only touches the latest commit and creates a new ID, which also rewrites published history.

options.text: `git restore --source=HEAD~1 .` then `git stash`
options.why: Stashing the restored files hides them; nothing is undone on the branch or the remote.

explanation: `git revert` records a new commit whose diff is the opposite of the target. History is preserved, so collaborators simply pull it. Resetting and force-pushing rewrites commits others are building on.
reference: Pro Git: Undoing Things; git-revert documentation

stem: Match each command with what it undoes.

options.text: Discards unstaged edits to a tracked file
Unstages a file but keeps its edits
Adds a new commit that cancels an earlier one
Deletes untracked files from the working tree

explanation: `restore` without flags copies from the index into the working tree; `--staged` copies from HEAD into the index; `revert` creates an inverse commit; `clean -f` removes files Git does not track.

stem: On a fresh Git installation you run `git clean` with no flags in a repo that has untracked files. What happens?

options.text: It deletes every untracked file except those matched by `.gitignore`
options.why: That is `git clean -f`; the bare command refuses to delete anything.

options.text: It lists the untracked files that would be removed, like a dry run
options.why: Listing is what `-n` / `--dry-run` does; the bare command errors out instead.

options.text: It refuses with `clean.requireForce is true and -f not given`
options.why: Because the default `clean.requireForce=true` demands `-f`, `-n` or `-i`.

options.text: It deletes untracked files and moves them to the stash first
options.why: git clean never stashes; deleted untracked files are gone for good.

explanation: `git clean` is destructive and cannot be undone, so `clean.requireForce` defaults to true. Git 2.55 prints `fatal: clean.requireForce is true and -f not given: refusing to clean`. Preview with `git clean -n` before `git clean -f`.

stem: Your working tree has no changes to tracked files, only a new untracked file `notes.md`. You run `git stash`. What happens?

options.text: Git prints "No local changes to save" and nothing is stashed
options.why: Plain stash ignores untracked files, so there is nothing to save.

options.text: `notes.md` is stashed and removed from the working tree until you pop
options.why: That needs `-u`; without it untracked files are never stashed.

options.text: An empty stash entry is created and `notes.md` stays
options.why: Git does not create empty stash entries; it reports nothing to save.

options.text: Git stages `notes.md` automatically and stashes it
options.why: Stash never stages untracked files on its own.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: `git stash` with only untracked files prints `No local changes to save`. Use `git stash -u` to include untracked files.

stem: You edited the tracked file `app.js` but have not staged it. Which commands throw away those working-tree edits? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git restore app.js`
options.why: Restores the working-tree copy from the index, discarding the unstaged edits.

options.text: `git checkout -- app.js`
options.why: The older spelling of the same operation: copy the index version over the file.

options.text: `git reset app.js`
options.why: Path-limited reset only rewrites the index entry; the working-tree edits remain.

options.text: `git clean -f app.js`
options.why: clean only removes untracked files, and `app.js` is tracked.

options.text: `git revert app.js`
options.why: revert takes commits, not paths, and never touches uncommitted edits.

explanation: `git restore <path>` (Git 2.23+) and `git checkout -- <path>` both overwrite the working tree from the index. These edits were never committed or staged, so they cannot be recovered afterwards.

stem: History is `c1 ← c2 ← c3` on `main`. `c2` modified `a.txt` and `c3` added `b.txt`. The working tree is clean. You run `git reset --soft HEAD~2`. What does `git status --short` show?

options.text: ` M a.txt` and `?? b.txt`
options.why: That is the result of a mixed reset, which also resets the index.

options.text: `M  a.txt` and `A  b.txt`
options.why: Soft reset moves only the branch; the index still holds c3, so both changes appear staged.

options.text: Nothing, because the working tree is clean
options.why: The working tree matches c3, but HEAD is now c1, so there are differences to show.

options.text: `D  b.txt` only
options.why: b.txt still exists in both the index and the working tree; nothing is deleted.

explanation: `--soft` moves the branch pointer and leaves the index and working tree alone. Compared with the new HEAD (c1), the index contains c2 and c3's changes, so they show as staged (`M ` and `A `). Running `git commit` now would squash c2 and c3 into one commit. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: The last commit modified `a.txt` and added the new file `b.txt`. You run `git reset HEAD~1` (no mode flag). What does `git status --short` show?

options.text: `M  a.txt` and `A  b.txt`
options.why: Those staged entries come from a soft reset; the default mode also resets the index.

options.text: A clean tree: the commit and its changes are gone
options.why: Discarding the changes needs `--hard`; the default keeps the working tree.

options.text: ` M a.txt` and `?? b.txt`
options.why: Mixed reset matches the index to HEAD~1, so a.txt is unstaged and b.txt becomes untracked.

options.text: ` M a.txt` and ` A b.txt`
options.why: There is no unstaged-add state: a file absent from the index is simply untracked.

explanation: The default mode is `--mixed`: the branch and the index move to HEAD~1 while the working tree keeps the newer content. A file that existed only in the undone commit is no longer in the index, so it shows as untracked (`??`). Verified with Git 2.55.

stem:
You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~2` and immediately regretted it. `git reflog` shows:

```text
a926a95 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
bfe93fb HEAD@{1}: commit: c3
4667a6a HEAD@{2}: commit: c2
a926a95 HEAD@{3}: commit (initial): c1
```

Which command restores the branch to where it was?

options.text: `git reset --hard HEAD@{2}`
options.why: HEAD@{2} is c2, one commit short of where the branch was.

options.text: `git revert HEAD@{0}`
options.why: Reflog entries are not commits to revert; the reset left no commit behind.

options.text: `git reset --hard HEAD~2` a second time
options.why: That moves two more commits back from c1 and fails, as c1 has no parents.

options.text: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`
options.why: HEAD@{1} is where HEAD pointed just before the reset: c3.

explanation: `HEAD@{n}` means "where HEAD was n moves ago". The entry before the reset is `bfe93fb` (c3), so `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`, or the SHA, or `ORIG_HEAD`, brings c2 and c3 back. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: You force-deleted a local branch with `git branch -D topic` and need it back. Put the recovery steps in order.

options.text: Run `git reflog` (or read the "Deleted branch topic (was …)" message) to find the tip commit
Identify the entry such as `commit: topic work` and copy its SHA
Recreate the branch with `git branch topic <sha>`
Check the result with `git log --oneline topic`

explanation: Deleting a branch removes the ref and its own reflog, but the commits still exist and the HEAD reflog remembers them. `git branch -D` even prints the old tip: `Deleted branch topic (was 41561c4)`. Pointing a new branch at that SHA restores it. Verified with Git 2.55.

stem: `git stash pop` hits a conflict in `a.txt`. What state are you in afterwards?

options.text: The pop is rolled back automatically and the stash is dropped
options.why: Git leaves the conflict for you to resolve; it does not roll back or drop.

options.text: `a.txt` shows as `UU` and the stash entry is kept in `git stash list`
options.why: Git only drops the entry after a clean apply, so it keeps it when a conflict occurs.

options.text: The stash is dropped right away and `a.txt` simply holds the stashed version
options.why: A conflicting pop never drops the entry and writes conflict markers instead.

options.text: Git refuses to start and asks for `git stash pop --force`
options.why: There is no `--force` for pop; it applies and reports the conflict.

explanation: Git 2.55 prints `CONFLICT (content)` and then "The stash entry is kept in case you need it again." After resolving, stage the file and run `git stash drop` yourself.

stem: When you push a branch, its reflog is pushed too, so a teammate can recover commits you reset away by reading your reflog on their clone.

options.text: True
options.why: Reflogs are never transferred by push, fetch or clone.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the reflog lives only in your repository's .git/logs, so each clone has its own.

explanation: Reflogs record how refs moved in this repository. They are local and expire (by default 90 days for reachable entries and 30 days for unreachable ones). A teammate can only recover commits that exist in their clone.

stem: You staged a change to `a.txt` and also have an unstaged change to `b.txt`. You run `git stash push --keep-index`. What is left in your working tree, and what is in the stash?

options.text: The tree is clean; the stash holds only `b.txt`
options.why: keep-index leaves the staged change in place rather than cleaning everything.

options.text: Only `b.txt` stays modified; the stash holds `a.txt`
options.why: That reverses the roles: the staged change stays, the unstaged one goes.

options.text: `a.txt` stays staged; the stash holds both changes
options.why: The stash records everything, and `--keep-index` then restores what was staged.

options.text: Both stay; `--keep-index` only copies the index into the stash
options.why: The unstaged `b.txt` change is removed from the working tree.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: after `git stash push --keep-index`, `git status` shows `M  a.txt`, `b.txt` is back at its committed content, and `git stash show --name-only` lists both files. It is handy for testing exactly what you are about to commit.

stem: In a repository with existing commits you ran `git add notes.md` on a brand-new file and want to unstage it without deleting it. Which commands work? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git restore --staged notes.md`
options.why: Removes the new entry from the index, so the file is untracked again.

options.text: `git rm --cached notes.md`
options.why: Drops the path from the index only, keeping the file on disk.

options.text: `git reset --hard`
options.why: A staged new file is tracked by the index, so hard reset deletes it from disk.

options.text: `git checkout -- notes.md`
options.why: This copies the index version over the file, so it stays staged.

options.text: `git clean -f notes.md`
options.why: The file is in the index, so clean treats it as tracked and skips it.

explanation: Both `restore --staged` and `rm --cached` leave `?? notes.md` in `git status`. Be careful with `reset --hard`: verified with Git 2.55, it deleted a staged-but-never-committed file.

stem: Your repo has an untracked directory `tmp/` containing files. `git clean -f` removes untracked files but leaves `tmp/` alone. Which flag do you add so it also removes untracked directories? Type the flag.
explanation: `git clean` only recurses into untracked directories when you pass `-d`. Verified with Git 2.55: `git clean -n` listed `u.txt` while `git clean -nd` also listed `newdir/`. Add `-x` to include ignored files too, or `-X` for ignored files only.

stem: Match each `git reset <commit>` mode with what it changes.

options.text: Moves the branch only; index and working tree keep the old content
Moves the branch and the index; the working tree is untouched
Moves the branch, the index and the working tree, discarding tracked changes
Moves branch, index and tree, but refuses if it would lose local changes

explanation: The modes differ in how far down the three trees the reset reaches. `--keep` is a safer `--hard`: it updates files changed between the commits only when you have no local edits to them, and aborts otherwise.

stem: `a.txt` is clean. You run `git checkout HEAD~1 -- a.txt`. What happens?

options.text: HEAD detaches at HEAD~1 and `a.txt` shows its old content
options.why: With a path after `--`, checkout does not move HEAD at all.

options.text: `a.txt` gets the HEAD~1 content in both the index and the working tree
options.why: The old version is staged and on disk; HEAD and the branch stay where they were.

options.text: Only the working tree changes, so `git status` shows ` M a.txt` afterwards
options.why: That is `git restore --source=HEAD~1`; checkout with a commit also updates the index.

options.text: Git refuses because `a.txt` has no local changes to restore
options.why: There is no such check; checkout overwrites the path from the given commit.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: after `git checkout HEAD~1 -- a.txt`, the file held the old text and `git status --short` showed `M  a.txt` (staged). Committing now records the old content as a new commit.

stem:
Starting from a clean tree, you restore an old version of `a.txt` two different ways (resetting between tries):

```bash
git restore --source=HEAD~1 a.txt   # try 1
git checkout HEAD~1 -- a.txt        # try 2
```

What does `git status --short` show after each?

options.text: Both show `M  a.txt`, staged in each of the two tries
options.why: restore without `--staged` writes only to the working tree, so try 1 is unstaged.

options.text: Try 1 shows `M  a.txt`; try 2 shows ` M a.txt`
options.why: That swaps them: checkout with a commit is the one that also writes the index.

options.text: Try 1 shows ` M a.txt`; try 2 shows `M  a.txt`
options.why: restore defaults to the working tree only; checkout writes the index and the tree.

options.text: Both show ` M a.txt`
options.why: checkout `<commit> -- path` also updates the index, so try 2 is staged.

explanation: `git restore --source=<commit> <path>` targets the working tree unless you add `--staged` (or both with `--staged --worktree`). The older `git checkout <commit> -- <path>` always updates the index as well. Both outputs verified with Git 2.55.

stem: Before running `git reset --hard`, your tree has: an edited tracked file `a.txt`, an untracked file `scratch.txt`, an ignored `debug.log`, and a new file `feature.ts` that you `git add`-ed but never committed. Which of these files exist afterwards?

options.text: `a.txt` (committed content), `scratch.txt` and `debug.log`
options.why: feature.ts was only in the index, so reset removes it; untracked and ignored files stay.

options.text: All four, with `feature.ts` back to untracked
options.why: Hard reset deletes index-only files from disk rather than unstaging them.

options.text: Only `a.txt`, since a hard reset cleans every other file
options.why: Untracked and ignored files are left alone; only git clean deletes them.

options.text: `a.txt`, `scratch.txt` and `feature.ts`, but not `debug.log`
options.why: reset never looks at ignored files, and the staged new file is the one removed.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: after `reset --hard`, the directory contained `.gitignore`, `a.txt`, `scratch.txt` (untracked) and the ignored log, while the staged-new file was gone. Its content survives only as a dangling blob (`git fsck --lost-found`).

stem: You try to undo a merge commit on `main` with `git revert HEAD` (HEAD is the merge). What happens?

options.text: Git reverts the whole feature branch's commits one by one
options.why: revert works on a single commit and needs to know which parent to diff against.

options.text: The merge is reverted relative to the first parent automatically
options.why: Git does not guess a mainline; it requires `-m` to be explicit.

options.text: It fails: "is a merge but no -m option was given"
options.why: A merge has two parents, so you must say which one is the mainline, usually `-m 1`.

options.text: It creates an empty revert commit, as merges contain no changes
options.why: Merges do introduce changes relative to each parent; Git still needs `-m`.

explanation: Git 2.55 prints `error: commit 3b40f11… is a merge but no -m option was given.` and `fatal: revert failed`. `git revert -m 1 <merge>` undoes everything the merge brought in relative to its first parent (main).

stem: You merged `feature` into `main`, found a bug, and reverted the merge with `git revert -m 1 <merge>`. Without adding any commits to `feature`, you now run `git merge feature` again. What happens?

options.text: All of feature's changes are applied again
options.why: The feature commits are already in main's history, so there is nothing new to merge.

options.text: Git says "Already up to date." and the changes stay reverted
options.why: Merge works on commits, and those commits are already reachable from main.

options.text: A conflict, because the revert deleted feature's files
options.why: With no new commits on feature, Git never reaches content merging; there is no conflict.

options.text: Git refuses to merge any branch whose earlier merge has been reverted
options.why: There is no such rule; the merge simply has nothing to do.

explanation: A revert undoes the content of a merge but not its history. Feature's commits are still ancestors of main, so a new merge has nothing to bring in. Verified with Git 2.55: `Already up to date.` To bring the work back, revert the revert.
reference: Git docs: How to revert a faulty merge

stem: After reverting a bad merge of `feature` (which added `f.txt`), the team fixes the bug with a new commit on `feature` that edits `f.txt`. Merging `feature` into `main` now produces `CONFLICT (modify/delete): f.txt deleted in HEAD and modified in feature`. What is the recommended way to land the fixed feature?

options.text: Resolve by keeping the feature version of `f.txt` and moving on
options.why: That restores only f.txt; other changes the revert removed stay missing.

options.text: Delete and recreate `feature` from main before merging
options.why: The old commits would still count as merged; the reverted changes stay gone.

options.text: Use `git merge -X theirs feature` to force feature's side
options.why: The strategy option only resolves this hunk; earlier reverted changes stay reverted.

options.text: Abort, `git revert` the revert commit, then merge `feature`
options.why: Reapplying the revert restores the original changes, so only the fix is merged.

explanation: Main still contains the revert, which deleted `f.txt`, while feature now modifies it. Reverting the revert (Git 2.43+ titles it `Reapply "…"`) puts the original changes back, and the follow-up merge brings only the new fix commits. Both outcomes reproduced with Git 2.55.
reference: Git docs: How to revert a faulty merge

stem: Right after an accidental `git reset --hard HEAD~3`, which of these can you still recover? (Choose two.)

options.text: The three commits the branch no longer points to
options.why: They still exist, and HEAD@{1} in the reflog points at the old tip.

options.text: Content of a new file you had staged but never committed
options.why: Staging wrote a blob, which `git fsck --lost-found` reports as dangling.

options.text: Edits you had made to a tracked file but never staged
options.why: Unstaged edits were never written to the object database, so they are gone.

options.text: The reflog entries from before the reset, which reset clears
options.why: reset adds a new reflog entry; it does not delete earlier ones.

options.text: Stash entries, which the hard reset drops along with the commits
options.why: Stashes live on refs/stash and are untouched by reset.

explanation: Git only keeps what reached the object database. Commits are found via `git reflog` or `ORIG_HEAD`. Staged content exists as a blob, and `git fsck --lost-found` reported it as a `dangling blob` in a Git 2.55 test. Edits that were never staged had no object and cannot be recovered.

stem: HEAD is `c2`, where `a.txt` contains `v2` (it was `v1` in `c1`). The tree is clean. You run `git reset HEAD~1 -- a.txt`. What is the result?

options.text: The branch moves to c1 and `a.txt` reads `v1`
options.why: With a path, reset never moves the branch or touches the working tree.

options.text: Only the working tree changes: `a.txt` reads `v1` and `git status` shows ` M a.txt`
options.why: Path reset updates the index, not the working tree.

options.text: HEAD stays at c2, the index holds `v1`, the file still reads `v2`: `MM a.txt`
options.why: Only the index entry changes, so it differs from both HEAD and the working tree.

options.text: Git refuses: reset needs a mode flag when given a path
options.why: Path-limited reset is valid; it is `--soft` and `--hard` that reject paths.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: `git status --short` showed `MM a.txt`. The staged change reverts a.txt to v1, and the unstaged change re-applies v2. HEAD stayed at `c2`. This is how you prepare a commit that undoes one file's change.

stem: What does `git reset --soft HEAD~1 -- a.txt` do?

options.text: Moves the branch back one commit but only for `a.txt`
options.why: Branches point at whole commits; there is no per-file branch position.

options.text: Stages the HEAD~1 version of `a.txt`, leaving everything else alone
options.why: That is what plain `git reset HEAD~1 -- a.txt` does; soft is refused.

options.text: Same as `git restore --source=HEAD~1 a.txt`
options.why: restore writes the working tree; this command errors before doing anything.

options.text: It fails with "Cannot do soft reset with paths."
options.why: Soft reset only moves the branch, which can't be done for a single path.

explanation: Git 2.55 prints `fatal: Cannot do soft reset with paths.` `--hard` with paths is rejected too. Path-limited reset always behaves like mixed, updating only the index entries.

stem: Your branch has three local "wip" commits on top of `origin/main`, none pushed. Put the steps to squash them into one commit with reset in order.

options.text: Confirm they are unpushed, for example with `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`
Run `git reset --soft HEAD~3`
Check `git status`: the combined changes are all staged
Run `git commit -m "Add feature"` to create the single commit

explanation: A soft reset rewinds the branch three commits but keeps their combined result in the index, so one new commit captures all of it. Checking they are unpushed first matters: squashing published commits rewrites shared history. Verified with Git 2.55: three wip commits became one, and the file kept its final content.

stem: History is `c1 ← c2 ← c3 ← c4` (HEAD). You run `git revert --no-edit HEAD~2..HEAD`. What happens?

options.text: One single commit reverts c2, c3 and c4 together
options.why: The range excludes HEAD~2 (c2), and revert makes one commit per target by default.

options.text: Two commits: `Revert "c4"`, then `Revert "c3"`
options.why: The range is c3 and c4, reverted newest first so each applies cleanly.

options.text: Two commits: `Revert "c3"`, then `Revert "c4"`
options.why: Reverting oldest first would fight later commits; Git reverts newest first.

options.text: Three commits reverting c2, c3 and c4
options.why: `A..B` excludes A, so c2 is not part of the range.

explanation: `HEAD~2..HEAD` means commits reachable from HEAD but not from HEAD~2: c3 and c4. Revert walks them in reverse, creating `Revert "c4"` and then `Revert "c3"`, as a Git 2.55 run showed. Add `--no-commit` to combine them into one commit.

stem: `git revert --no-commit HEAD~2..HEAD` creates two revert commits but leaves them unpublished until you push.

options.text: True
options.why: With --no-commit Git creates no commits; it only applies the inverse changes.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the combined inverse changes are left staged, and nothing is committed until you commit.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: after `--no-commit`, the commit count was unchanged and `git status` showed both reversions staged. Commit once to get a single revert, or run `git revert --abort` to back out.

stem:
A repo has this `.gitignore`:

```text
build/
*.log
```

Untracked items: `u.txt`, `newdir/n.txt`, `build/o.bin`, `x.log`. Which entries does `git clean -ndX` list? (Choose two.)

options.text: `build/`
options.why: An ignored directory, and `-X` removes only ignored paths (`-d` lets it take directories).

options.text: `x.log`
options.why: An ignored file, so `-X` selects it.

options.text: `u.txt`
options.why: Untracked but not ignored, and `-X` (capital) skips non-ignored files.

options.text: `newdir/`
options.why: An untracked, non-ignored directory; only lowercase `-x` or no -x/-X would include it.

options.text: `.gitignore`
options.why: It is tracked (committed), so clean never touches it.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: `git clean -ndX` printed "Would remove build/" and "Would remove x.log". Lowercase `-x` removes untracked and ignored files together; capital `-X` removes only ignored ones, handy for wiping build output while keeping new source files.

stem: HEAD (`c2`) changed `a.txt` relative to `c1`. You have an uncommitted edit to `a.txt`. You run `git reset --keep HEAD~1`. What happens?

options.text: The branch moves to c1 and your edit to `a.txt` is discarded
options.why: That is `--hard`; `--keep` exists precisely to avoid losing such edits.

options.text: It aborts with "Entry 'a.txt' not uptodate. Cannot merge."
options.why: a.txt differs between the commits and has local edits, so keep refuses.

options.text: The branch moves and your edit is kept, conflicting with c1
options.why: keep never leaves conflicts; it either succeeds cleanly or refuses.

options.text: It behaves like `--soft`, keeping both versions staged
options.why: keep updates the index and working tree like hard, unless that would lose edits.

explanation: Git 2.55 printed `error: Entry 'a.txt' not uptodate. Cannot merge.` and left everything unchanged. When the local edit was to a file the two commits did not change (`b.txt`), `--keep` succeeded and kept the edit.

stem: You ran `git stash -u` with a modified `a.txt` and a new untracked `u.txt`. `git stash show --name-only` prints only `a.txt`. Where is `u.txt`?

options.text: It was not stashed; `-u` only stages untracked files
options.why: -u does stash untracked files; they are removed from the tree and saved.

options.text: It was deleted, since stash cannot store untracked files
options.why: Untracked files are stored, in a separate commit.

options.text: In the index of the stash commit, which plain `stash show` never displays
options.why: The stash's index parent holds staged changes; untracked files are elsewhere.

options.text: In the stash's third parent; `show --include-untracked` lists it
options.why: With `-u` the stash commit gets a third parent holding the untracked files.

explanation: A stash is a merge-like commit: parent 1 is HEAD, parent 2 records the index, and with `-u` (or `-a`) parent 3 stores untracked files. Verified with Git 2.55: the stash had 3 parents, plain `stash show` listed `a.txt`, and `--include-untracked` added `u.txt`.

stem: A merge stops with conflicts in `a.txt`. Before starting it you had an unrelated, uncommitted edit to `b.txt` that you want to keep. Which command abandons the merge and keeps the `b.txt` edit?

options.text: `git reset --hard` to throw away the half-done merge
options.why: It abandons the merge but also discards the unrelated b.txt edit.

options.text: `git restore .` across the whole working tree
options.why: It cannot restore unmerged paths, and it would also revert b.txt.

options.text: `git stash` to set the conflicted merge state aside
options.why: Stash refuses while unmerged paths exist and wouldn't end the merge.

options.text: `git reset --merge` (or `git merge --abort`)
options.why: It resets merge-touched entries and keeps local edits to other files.

explanation: `--merge` resets the index and the files that differ between ORIG_HEAD and HEAD, but leaves entries with local changes the merge never touched. Verified with Git 2.55: after `git reset --merge`, `a.txt` was back to main's version and `b.txt` still had the local edit. `git merge --abort` uses the same mechanism.

stem: `main` gained `m.txt` in its own commit, then merged `feature`, which added `f.txt`. You run `git revert --no-edit -m 2 <merge>`. Which files remain afterwards?

options.text: Only main's files; `f.txt` is removed
options.why: That is `-m 1`, which treats main as the mainline and undoes feature's side.

options.text: `f.txt` remains and `m.txt` is removed
options.why: With parent 2 as the mainline, Git undoes what main had relative to feature.

options.text: Both stay, as `-m 2` only rewrites the merge message
options.why: -m picks the mainline parent and changes which side gets undone.

options.text: Neither: `-m 2` reverts both sides of the merge
options.why: Revert diffs against one parent, so only one side's changes are undone.

explanation: `-m N` names the parent to treat as the mainline, and the revert undoes the merge's diff against that parent. With `-m 2` (feature's tip), that diff is main's own work, so `m.txt` disappears. Verified with Git 2.55: the tree held `a.txt` and `f.txt`. That is almost never what you want; `-m 1` is the usual choice.

stem: You ran `git branch -D topic`, then tried `git reflog show topic` to find its old tip. Git answered `fatal: ambiguous argument 'topic'`. Why, and what still works?

options.text: Its reflog was deleted with it; use the HEAD reflog or the printed SHA
options.why: Deleting a ref removes its log, but HEAD's reflog still records the topic commits.

options.text: Its reflog only exists after `git gc`; run gc and retry
options.why: gc prunes reflogs rather than creating them, and could lose the commits sooner.

options.text: The commits were deleted with the branch; only a remote copy can save you
options.why: Deleting a branch never deletes commits; they stay until gc prunes them.

options.text: `reflog show` needs `refs/heads/topic` spelled out to work
options.why: The full name fails the same way because the log file is gone.

explanation: Each ref has its own reflog under `.git/logs/`, removed when the ref is deleted. In a Git 2.55 test, HEAD's reflog still listed `commit: topic work`, and `git branch -D` had printed `(was 41561c4)`, so `git branch topic <sha>` restored it.

stem: Which statements about the reflog are true for a default Git 2.4x setup? (Choose three.)

options.text: Entries for commits still reachable from the ref expire after 90 days
options.why: gc.reflogExpire defaults to 90 days.

options.text: Entries for commits no longer reachable from the ref expire after 30 days
options.why: gc.reflogExpireUnreachable defaults to 30 days, which bounds how long a bad reset can be undone.

options.text: Deleting a branch deletes that branch's reflog
options.why: The ref's log file is removed with it; HEAD's reflog remains.

options.text: `git push` sends the reflog so collaborators share it
options.why: Reflogs are local and never transferred.

options.text: Every `git gc` run empties the reflog completely
options.why: gc only expires entries older than the configured limits.

options.text: The reflog records uncommitted working-tree edits too
options.why: It only records where refs pointed, never uncommitted edits.

explanation: The reflog is a local safety net: it logs ref movements, and `git gc` (through `git reflog expire`) prunes entries older than 90 or 30 days. Once an unreachable commit loses its last reflog entry, a later gc may delete the object for good.

stem: You had `a.txt` staged when you ran `git stash`. After `git stash pop`, `git status --short` shows ` M a.txt` (unstaged). How do you restore the staged state too?

options.text: Nothing: stash never records what was staged
options.why: It does record the index, in the stash commit's second parent.

options.text: Use `git stash apply --keep-index`
options.why: --keep-index is an option of push, not apply, and does a different job.

options.text: Pop with `git stash pop --index`
options.why: --index re-applies the saved index too, so `a.txt` comes back as `M  a.txt`.

options.text: Run `git stash show -p | git apply` instead of pop
options.why: git apply without --index or --cached only touches the working tree.

explanation: By default apply and pop merge only the working-tree changes, so anything staged comes back unstaged. Verified with Git 2.55: plain pop gave ` M a.txt`, while `pop --index` gave `M  a.txt`. `--index` can fail if the index changes conflict.

stem: In a brand-new repository with **no commits yet**, you ran `git add a.txt`. Which command unstages it?

options.text: `git restore --staged a.txt`
options.why: It fails with "could not resolve 'HEAD'": there is no HEAD commit to restore from.

options.text: `git reset HEAD a.txt`
options.why: It fails because HEAD is not a valid revision on an unborn branch.

options.text: `git rm --cached a.txt`
options.why: It only removes the index entry, which needs no HEAD commit.

options.text: `git checkout HEAD -- a.txt`
options.why: It fails with "invalid reference: HEAD" before any commit exists.

explanation: On an unborn branch HEAD points to a branch that does not exist yet, so commands that read from HEAD fail. Verified with Git 2.55: `restore --staged` and `reset HEAD` failed, while `rm --cached` left `?? a.txt`. Plain `git reset a.txt` also works, as Git special-cases the unborn branch.

stem: History: `c1` added the line `line1`, `c2` changed it to `line1 edited`, and `c3` changed it to `line1 edited again`. `git revert HEAD~1` (reverting c2) stops with a conflict. Why, and how do you return to where you were?

options.text: Revert can only undo HEAD; use `git revert HEAD` instead
options.why: revert accepts any commit; the conflict comes from overlapping changes.

options.text: c2 was already reverted by c3; run `git revert --skip` to finish the operation cleanly
options.why: c3 did not revert c2; it edited the same line again.

options.text: The repo is corrupted; run `git fsck` and then retry
options.why: This is an ordinary content conflict, not corruption.

options.text: c3 overlaps the line c2 changed; `git revert --abort` restores your state
options.why: The inverse of c2 overlaps c3's edit, so abort leaves `line1 edited again`.

explanation: Reverting is a three-way merge of c2's inverse onto HEAD. A later commit touching the same lines makes it conflict. Git 2.55 showed `UU a.txt`, and `git revert --abort` put the file back to `line1 edited again`. Otherwise you resolve, `git add`, and `git revert --continue`.

stem: You ran `git stash drop` on the wrong entry, which held important work. No new stash was created since. How can you recover it?

options.text: `git reflog` on HEAD, then reset to the stash entry
options.why: Stash commits are on refs/stash, not HEAD's reflog, and resetting would be wrong.

options.text: It is unrecoverable, because drop deletes the stash commit object immediately and for good
options.why: drop only removes the ref; the commit object remains until gc prunes it.

options.text: Run `git stash pop` again, which restores the last dropped entry
options.why: pop applies the current top entry; it has no memory of dropped ones.

options.text: Find the dangling commit with `git fsck --lost-found`, then `git stash apply <sha>`
options.why: The dropped stash commit becomes a dangling commit object that you can still apply.

explanation: `git stash drop` prints the SHA it dropped (`Dropped refs/stash@{0} (<sha>)`), so check your scrollback first. Otherwise, in a Git 2.55 test, `git fsck --lost-found` listed it as a `dangling commit`, and `git stash apply <sha>` brings it back. Act before `git gc` prunes unreachable objects.

stem: You pushed `c2` to `origin/main`, then ran `git reset --hard HEAD~1` locally to "undo" it. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: A plain `git push origin main` is rejected as non-fast-forward
options.why: Your branch is now behind the remote, so pushing would discard c2 there.

options.text: `git status -sb` shows `## main...origin/main [behind 1]`
options.why: The local branch lost c2 while origin/main still points at it.

options.text: The push succeeds and removes `c2` for every teammate
options.why: Git rejects it, and even a forced push leaves c2 in other clones.

options.text: Your reflog is synced to the remote, so others can undo it
options.why: Reflogs are never pushed.

options.text: You can no longer use `git revert`, since c2 is gone locally
options.why: c2 still exists (reachable via origin/main), so you can revert it.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55 against a local bare remote: the push failed with `! [rejected] main -> main (non-fast-forward)`, and status reported `[behind 1]`. For published commits, `git reset --hard origin/main` then `git revert c2` is the clean fix.

stem: A merged `feature` broke production and was reverted with `git revert -m 1 <merge>`. The fix is ready. Put the steps to re-land the feature correctly in order.

options.text: Revert the merge on `main` with `git revert -m 1 <merge>`
Commit the bug fix on `feature`
On `main`, revert the revert commit (`git revert <revert-sha>`)
Merge `feature` into `main`, bringing in only the new fix

explanation: The first revert removes the merge's changes but leaves feature's commits in history. Reverting that revert restores them, after which merging `feature` brings in only the commits made since (the fix). Skipping the revert-the-revert leaves the original changes missing or produces modify/delete conflicts.
reference: Git docs: How to revert a faulty merge

stem: Match each situation with the most appropriate tool.

options.text: `git commit --amend`
`git revert`
`git reflog` + `git reset --hard <sha>`
`git stash`

explanation: Amend rewrites only an unpublished last commit. Revert is the shared-history-safe undo. The reflog is your local time machine after resets and rebases. Stash shelves uncommitted work temporarily.

prompts.text: Your last, unpushed commit has a typo in its message
A pushed commit on shared main broke production
You lost commits after an over-eager hard reset
Half-finished work must be set aside to fix an urgent bug

stem: In Git 2.43 and later, running `git revert` on a commit whose subject is `Revert "Add search"` creates a commit with a new subject. Type the word that this new subject starts with.
explanation: Since Git 2.43, reverting a revert produces `Reapply "Add search"` instead of the stacked `Revert "Revert "Add search""`. Verified with Git 2.55, which created `Reapply "merge feature"` when reverting a merge revert.
